title: You and yours are His (Avot 3:7)
hookLine: Elazar of Bartota: give Him of what is His, for you and all you have are His
tomorrow: why would a sage frown at someone admiring a tree?

lines: CAN I ASK YOU A QUICK QUESTION?
cards: Clipboards on a busy sidewalk, a volunteer calling out, can I ask you a quick question? The usual move is to speed up and study your phone. In one Talmud story it runs the other way: the collectors hide from the giver.

Elazar of Bartota gives so much, they duck when they see him coming. One day he's on his way to market with money for his daughter's wedding. The collectors spot him, and this time they can't get away.
They're raising money for an orphan couple's wedding. He asks what they need.

teach.h: ONE COIN, A STOREROOM OF WHEAT.
teach.b: He gives them nearly all of it. He keeps one small coin, buys a little wheat with it, and leaves it in the storeroom. In the story, when the storeroom is opened, it's filled with wheat.
The story's told with wonder, not as a rule that everyone must empty their pockets.

teach.h: GIVE HIM OF WHAT IS HIS.
teach.b: Avot keeps Elazar's teaching in a single line: give Him of what is His, for you and what is yours are His. That's the idea.
Nothing in the hand was ever fully ours, so giving isn't losing; it's handing something back to its owner.

teach.h: OF THINE OWN HAVE WE GIVEN THEE.
teach.b: He proves it from King David, collecting gifts to build the Temple, who prays: "for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee." Even David's generosity was only returning.
Second, the Hebrew for this kind of giving is tzedakah, often translated charity; some teachers stress that it's closer to justice.
Less a favor than setting things right. Third, the saying keeps the giver humble.
If it was all His, the giver isn't a hero. Fourth, it keeps the giver unafraid. If it was always His, there's no need to clutch.

how: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, called a pushke in Yiddish, and drop coins in before Shabbat; giving to people in need is counted among the commandments.

games.q: what does “you and yours are his” mean?
o: your possessions define who you really are
you owe your parents everything you ever earn
everything you have is God's, so giving is giving back

games.q: the giver and the line — tap the pairs.
p: of thine own have we given thee

s: in the Talmud, charity collectors hid when they saw Elazar coming
he'd give them everything he had.
'you and yours are His' means what you have is worthless
it means what you have is entrusted to you, and giving returns some of it.
David's line 'of thine own have we given thee' is in the book of Chronicles
1 Chronicles 29:14, as he collects gifts for the Temple.

games.q: you've saved for concert tickets, and a friend's fundraiser for a family in need lands the same week. by Elazar's saying, how do you see your savings?
o: as entrusted to you, so some can go back.
as fully yours; giving is only for when you're rich.
as all owed away, so you keep nothing at all.
games.why: Elazar's line treats what you hold as His, on loan. the story of his giving is told with wonder; the saying asks you to give of it, not to give it all.

practice: Open your hands, palms up, and count on your fingers things you have that you didn't make: this breath, this morning, a skill someone taught you, a friend. With each one, turn your palms a little higher.
At the end, choose one to give back this week, as time, as money, or as a kindness.

wordCard.voice: You and yours are His: Elazar of Bartota's line that everything we hold is held on loan, so giving is giving back.

orig.note: Hebrew: give Him of what is His, Avot 3:7.

carryVoice: The line to carry: you and yours are his, every coin and every hour. Good night.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:7 (Rabbi Elazar of Bartota)
